title: How do you capture a thread dump and how do you read it? Explain jstack, kill -3 and jcmd, and how to interpret thread name, state, stack trace, lock ownership, and the deadlock section.
shortTitle: How to capture and read a thread dump?

s1_definition.profdef: A thread dump is a snapshot of every thread in a JVM at one moment, showing each thread's name, state, call stack, and the locks it holds or is waiting on. You capture it with `jstack <pid>`, by sending the quit signal via `kill -3 <pid>` (which prints the dump to the process's standard output), or with `jcmd <pid> Thread.print`. You read it to diagnose hangs, high CPU, and deadlocks: a thread stuck in BLOCKED is waiting for a monitor another thread holds, a thread in WAITING or TIMED_WAITING is parked, and the JVM prints an explicit deadlock section when two threads hold locks each other needs.
s1_definition.analogy: A thread dump is like freezing time in National Bank of India and photographing every teller at once: what each is doing, which vault key they are holding, and which key they are waiting for. If teller A is holding the gold-vault key but waiting for the cash-vault key, while teller B holds the cash-vault key but waits for the gold-vault key, neither can move. The photograph shows you exactly that frozen standoff, which is a deadlock.
s1_definition.oneliner: Capture a thread dump with jstack, kill -3, or jcmd, then read each thread's state and lock ownership to find the stuck thread or the deadlock section.
s1_definition.raw:
**Professional definition:** A thread dump is a snapshot of every thread in a JVM at one moment, showing each thread's name, state, call stack, and the locks it holds or is waiting on. You capture it with `jstack <pid>`, by sending the quit signal via `kill -3 <pid>` (which prints the dump to the process's standard output), or with `jcmd <pid> Thread.print`. You read it to diagnose hangs, high CPU, and deadlocks: a thread stuck in BLOCKED is waiting for a monitor another thread holds, a thread in WAITING or TIMED_WAITING is parked, and the JVM prints an explicit deadlock section when two threads hold locks each other needs.

**In simple words (banking analogy):** A thread dump is like freezing time in National Bank of India and photographing every teller at once: what each is doing, which vault key they are holding, and which key they are waiting for. If teller A is holding the gold-vault key but waiting for the cash-vault key, while teller B holds the cash-vault key but waits for the gold-vault key, neither can move. The photograph shows you exactly that frozen standoff, which is a deadlock.

**One line to remember:** Capture a thread dump with jstack, kill -3, or jcmd, then read each thread's state and lock ownership to find the stuck thread or the deadlock section.

sections.s2_technical:
To capture a dump, `jstack <pid>` is the most common tool; it attaches to the process and prints all thread stacks. `jstack -l <pid>` adds extra lock information including ownable synchronizers like ReentrantLock. Finding the pid is easy with `jps`. On a running server, `kill -3 <pid>` (also called SIGQUIT) tells the JVM to print a thread dump to its own standard output or console log, which is handy when you cannot attach a tool. `jcmd <pid> Thread.print` is the modern, preferred way and also supports `-l` for lock details.

Reading a dump starts with the thread name. A good name like `payment-worker-3` tells you which subsystem is involved, which is why naming your threads matters. Next is the state. RUNNABLE means executing or ready to execute (if many threads are RUNNABLE deep in your code, suspect high CPU). BLOCKED means the thread is waiting to acquire a monitor lock another thread holds. WAITING and TIMED_WAITING mean the thread is parked, for example in `Object.wait`, `LockSupport.park`, or `Thread.sleep`.

The stack trace shows what each thread is doing, top frame first. Below the stack you see lock lines. `- locked <0x...> (a com.bank.Account)` means this thread currently holds that monitor. `- waiting to lock <0x...> (a com.bank.Account)` means it is blocked trying to acquire a monitor some other thread holds. By matching the hex identity of the lock across threads, you can see exactly who holds what and who is waiting for it.

The deadlock section is the gold. When the JVM detects a cycle of threads each waiting on a lock another holds, it prints a block titled "Found one Java-level deadlock" listing the threads and the chain: thread A is waiting to lock a monitor held by thread B, which is waiting to lock a monitor held by thread A. This tells you precisely which code paths and which lock objects are involved, so you can fix the lock ordering.

A senior-level nuance is reading several dumps a few seconds apart. One dump is a snapshot; comparing two or three shows which threads are moving and which are stuck at the same frame, which distinguishes a genuine hang from normal busy work. For high CPU you combine a dump with native thread CPU from the operating system to map a hot OS thread id to a Java thread by its nid in the dump.
sections.s3_banking:
Problem 1 — National Bank of India's transfer service froze in production during peak load. No error was logged; requests simply hung. The on-call engineer needed to see what every thread was doing without restarting the service. This is exactly what a thread dump gives — a live snapshot of all threads and their locks.

Problem 2 — The freeze turned out to be a deadlock: a transfer from Rajesh to Priya locked Rajesh's account then tried to lock Priya's, while a simultaneous transfer from Priya to Rajesh locked Priya's then tried Rajesh's. This is exactly what the deadlock section of a thread dump reveals — the lock cycle and the two code paths.

The project reproduces a classic account-transfer deadlock so you can capture and read a real dump. `Account` has a lock. `TransferService.transfer` locks the from-account then the to-account. The demo starts two opposite transfers that deadlock, prints the process pid so you can run jstack, and a test uses the ThreadMXBean to assert the JVM detects the deadlock programmatically.

sections.s4e_build:
```bash
# Build
mvn clean package -DskipTests

# Run — it prints its PID, then hangs (the deadlock)
java -cp target/classes com.bank.diag.ThreadDumpDemo

# Capture a thread dump three ways (use the printed PID):
jstack -l <pid>                 # richest, with ownable synchronizers
jcmd <pid> Thread.print -l      # modern preferred tool
kill -3 <pid>                   # prints dump to the JVM's stdout/console log

# Run the test (asserts the JVM detects the deadlock)
mvn test -Dtest=DeadlockDetectionTest
```
sections.s5_journey:
Input: two threads, transfer-A moves 5000 from SAV2001 to CUR3001, transfer-B moves 3000 from CUR3001 to SAV2001, started at the same time.

Step 1 — transfer-A enters `transfer` and acquires the monitor on SAV2001's lock. transfer-B enters and acquires the monitor on CUR3001's lock. Both log that they hold one lock and want the other.

Step 2 — Both sleep 100 milliseconds, widening the window so each firmly holds its first lock before trying the second.

Step 3 — transfer-A tries to acquire CUR3001's monitor, which transfer-B holds, so transfer-A becomes BLOCKED. transfer-B tries to acquire SAV2001's monitor, which transfer-A holds, so transfer-B becomes BLOCKED. Neither can proceed.

Step 4 — The engineer runs `jstack -l <pid>`. The dump shows transfer-A "waiting to lock <0xAAA> (a java.lang.Object)" while "locked <0xBBB>", and transfer-B the mirror image, and then a "Found one Java-level deadlock" section naming both threads and the cycle.

Step 5 — The fix is to impose a global lock ordering, for example always lock the account with the smaller account id first, so both transfers acquire locks in the same order and the cycle cannot form.

Final output (abridged jstack):

```
Found one Java-level deadlock:
=============================
"transfer-A":
  waiting to lock monitor 0x... (a java.lang.Object),
  which is held by "transfer-B"
"transfer-B":
  waiting to lock monitor 0x... (a java.lang.Object),
  which is held by "transfer-A"

"transfer-A" #12 prio=5 BLOCKED
   at com.bank.diag.TransferService.transfer(TransferService.java:18)
   - waiting to lock <0xAAA> (a java.lang.Object)
   - locked <0xBBB> (a java.lang.Object)
```

```
  │     TransferService           │ locks  │        Account            │
  │  + transfer(from,to,amount)   │ ─────▶ │  - lock: Object           │
  │    synchronized(from.lock())  │        │  - balance: BigDecimal    │

                      ▼
  ┌───────────────────────────────┐
  │  ThreadMXBean (JDK)           │
  │  + findDeadlockedThreads()    │  mirrors dump's deadlock section
  └───────────────────────────────┘

  ── Thread States in a Dump ───────────────────────────────

  RUNNABLE      → executing / ready (many = high CPU)
  BLOCKED       → waiting for a monitor another thread holds
  WAITING       → parked (wait/park, no timeout)
  TIMED_WAITING → parked with timeout (sleep/wait(ms))

  How to read lock lines:
    - locked <0xBBB>           → this thread HOLDS the monitor
    - waiting to lock <0xAAA>  → this thread is BLOCKED on it
    match hex across threads   → reveals the cycle
```
sections.s6_takeaway:
A thread dump is a point-in-time snapshot of every thread inside a JVM, showing each thread's name, state, call stack, and the locks it is holding or waiting on. I capture it in one of three ways. The most common is jstack with the process id, and I add the minus l flag to get the extra lock information including ReentrantLock ownable synchronizers. On a running server where I cannot attach a tool I send the quit signal with kill minus 3, which makes the JVM print the dump to its own console log. The modern, preferred tool is jcmd with Thread.print, which also supports minus l for lock details.

When I read a dump I start with the thread name, which is why I always give my threads meaningful names like payment-worker-3, because that instantly tells me which subsystem is involved. Then I look at the state. RUNNABLE means executing or ready, and many RUNNABLE threads deep in my code suggests high CPU. BLOCKED means the thread is waiting for a monitor that another thread holds. WAITING and TIMED_WAITING mean the thread is parked, for example in wait, park, or sleep.

The most valuable parts are the lock lines and the deadlock section. A line saying locked followed by a hex identity means this thread holds that monitor, and a line saying waiting to lock means it is blocked trying to acquire a monitor someone else holds. By matching the hex identity of the lock across threads I can see exactly who holds what and who is waiting. When there is a true cycle, the JVM prints a section titled Found one Java-level deadlock that names the threads and the chain, which points me straight at the two code paths and the two lock objects. I usually also take two or three dumps a few seconds apart, because comparing them tells me which threads are genuinely stuck versus just busy.

At National Bank of India our transfer service once froze in production with no errors in the logs, and requests just hung. I ran jstack with minus l against the live process, and the deadlock section showed thread transfer-A holding Rajesh's account lock and waiting for Priya's, while transfer-B held Priya's and waited for Rajesh's, a classic lock-ordering cycle because the code always locked the from-account first. The fix was a global lock ordering, always locking the account with the smaller account id first, so both transfers acquire locks in the same order and the cycle can never form. The sentence I give interviewers is that I capture a thread dump with jstack, jcmd, or kill minus 3, then read each thread's state and its locked and waiting-to-lock lines, and the deadlock section tells me the exact lock cycle, which I resolve by imposing a consistent global lock ordering.
